title: Unsupervised and Association Learning
topicSummary: K-means, hierarchical clustering, PCA, dimensionality reduction, Apriori algorithm, Frequent pattern mining etc., Case studies.

content.text: This module focuses on learning patterns without labeled data and discovering hidden structures and relationships.
Objective: Group similar data (clustering), reduce complexity (dimensionality reduction), and discover patterns (association rules).
Definition: Unsupervised learning works on unlabeled data (no predefined output). The model finds patterns automatically.

📖 Reading Note: Unsupervised learning is most valuable in urban informatics when we don't know the 'answer' in advance. For example, the Delhi Urban Art Commission wanted to classify city neighborhoods into 'character zones' for heritage regulation. With no pre-labeled zones, they applied K-Means clustering on 22 urban morphology features (building height variance, road width, plot coverage ratio, green space %) across 200 neighborhoods. The algorithm discovered 6 natural clusters that planners named: Heritage Core, Transit Corridor, Residential Low Density, Industrial, etc. This unsupervised discovery shaped a new zoning policy.
Definition: K-Means groups data into K clusters based on similarity.

items: Applications: Grouping city zones, Identifying traffic patterns, Market segmentation.
Limitations: Need to choose K, sensitive to initial centroids.

content.text: 📖 Reading Note: Choosing the right K is done using the 'Elbow Method': run K-Means for K=2,3,4,...,10 and plot the total inertia (within-cluster sum of squares) for each K. The plot looks like an arm — inertia drops steeply then levels off. The 'elbow' (where the curve bends) is the optimal K. Example: For clustering Bengaluru's 198 wards by socioeconomic indicators, the elbow appears at K=5, revealing 5 natural ward tiers — which aligned closely with BBMP's own ward classification. Elbow method is the standard technique tested in exams.
Definition: Builds a tree-like structure (dendrogram) of clusters.

items: Advantages: No need to predefine K, Visual representation (dendrogram).

content.text: 📖 Reading Note: Hierarchical clustering is preferred over K-Means in urban ecology studies because it reveals nested relationships. Example: When classifying Mumbai's urban tree canopy by species composition, hierarchical clustering shows: at distance threshold 0.5, areas split into 'native forest' vs 'ornamental'; at threshold 0.8, native forest further splits into 'riparian' vs 'upland'. This multi-level hierarchy gives ecologists a richer picture than the flat grouping of K-Means. In Python: from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage then linkage(data, method='ward').
Definition: Reducing the number of features while preserving important information.
Why Needed? High-dimensional data is complex, improves performance and visualization.
Definition: PCA transforms data into new variables (principal components) capturing maximum variance.
Key Idea: Reduce dimensions while retaining most important information. Z = XW

📖 Reading Note: PCA is commonly used before clustering in urban data projects. Imagine you have 15 features describing each ward: population density, income, age distribution, commute times, green cover, crime rate, etc. Many of these are correlated (low income areas often have high crime AND low green cover). Feeding 15 correlated features into K-Means gives noisy, redundant clusters. Running PCA first reduces to 3 uncorrelated principal components that capture 85% of variance, then clustering on these 3 components gives cleaner, more meaningful urban typologies. PCA → Clustering is a standard pipeline in urban informatics research.
Definition: Find relationships between variables in large datasets.
Example: If high traffic + rain → high accident probability.
Definition: An algorithm used to find frequent itemsets and generate association rules.

📖 Reading Note: Association rule mining is powerful for urban infrastructure dependency analysis. A study of Kolkata's underground water pipe failures found: Rule {pipe_age > 30 years, soil_type = clay} → {pipe_failure within 6 months} with Support=0.35 and Confidence=0.82. This means 35% of all pipe data showed this pattern, and when both conditions were true, failure occurred 82% of the time. Kolkata Municipal Corporation used these rules to proactively replace high-risk pipes, reducing emergency failures by 28% in the first year — a direct ROI from association rule mining.
Definition: Finding patterns that occur frequently in datasets (e.g., peak traffic hours, frequent accident zones).

items: Urban Zone Classification: Hierarchical clustering of residential/commercial zones.
Accident Pattern Analysis: Apriori rules linking weather and traffic.
Pollution Data Reduction: PCA to reduce variables for analysis.

content.text: How Week 8 Concepts Connect Across the Course:

rows: K-Means is used to discover natural groupings in urban systems data (transport zones, ward typologies) — operationalizing Week 1's concept of urban interconnectedness
Bus route clustering in Week 12 uses K-Means to group high-demand corridors — a direct application of Week 8's clustering to public transport optimization
Before feeding high-dimensional sensor data into deep networks, PCA preprocessing reduces noise and speeds training — Week 8's PCA is a preprocessing step for Week 9
Association mining needs large transaction datasets — the data access techniques (SQL, APIs) from Week 3 are how you gather the data Apriori analyzes
Week 8 is the 'other half' of ML introduced in Week 6. Week 6–7 = supervised (predict with labels); Week 8 = unsupervised (discover without labels)
IoT devices generate streams of events — frequent pattern mining finds co-occurring sensor events (e.g., PM2.5 spike + traffic spike together) from Week 10's data streams

content.text: 🔗 Big Picture: Week 8 is where ML becomes exploratory science rather than engineering. While Weeks 6–7 answer 'What will happen?', Week 8 answers 'What is already happening that we don't know about?' — crucial for urban discovery projects where ground truth doesn't exist yet.
